name: Priya Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Priya, 58, an experienced mid-level developer at a tech company that makes timekeeping software for home-care agencies. I have a bachelor's degree, and I know the awkward overnight shifts even if I am not the fastest coder. I have never used an AI tool; I check a signed care sheet when the app puts a carer's minutes in the wrong day. My partner takes variable shifts at a laundry, our children are grown, and we rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell care workers the clock-in record needs to agree with the shift they actually worked. I maintain the home-care timekeeping software at a tech company, and when a visit runs past midnight I check the signed paper sheet before changing a wage total.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even with AI going nowhere, I worry about rent. I am 58 and experienced after a bachelor's degree, but the pay is low for this work; my partner's laundry shifts vary, we have about three weeks saved, and there are few similar software jobs nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reconciling overnight-shift bugs against signed care sheets. We'd cancel the 22 monthly film subscription and put that fee into a separate bill account whenever both of us are paid, then ask the landlord for a written due-date arrangement if the laundry shifts fall short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A quiet AI future does not make the rent wait for my partner's next rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened after midnight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One carer finished at 12:20 after starting before midnight, but the app put the last twenty minutes into the next day's unpaid break. The signed sheet showed the extra work, and I corrected the calculation before payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your children help with rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children have rent and work of their own. I would ask them to visit, not to carry our payroll gap.

say: I'd check **signed care sheets** before changing an overnight wage.
I'd keep **midnight shift errors** visible before payday.
think: I have **three weeks saved** against rent and variable laundry shifts.
I see **few local software jobs** even in a quiet AI world.
do: Keep **reconciling overnight shifts** against signed care sheets.
Cancel **film subscription** and save 22 monthly when both are paid; ask landlord about due date if laundry pay falls.
feel: **Anxious** about ordinary rent pressure despite little AI change.
S0.quote: A quiet AI future does not make the rent wait for my partner's next rota.
fieldNote: **Three weeks saved** and low pay keep baseline anxiety high, especially with variable laundry shifts.
Her experienced work is **wage reconciliation**, anchored to signed care sheets rather than AI drafts.

steps.text: Keep correcting overnight care shifts against signed paper sheets
Cancel monthly film subscription to protect rent cash
Save cancelled film fee monthly whenever both wages arrive

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI can write timekeeping code and answer staff pay questions, but a carer's missing twenty minutes is still missing money. I would ask the care agency for its signed sheet before accepting an automatic correction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My experience helps me spot a wrong wage, yet the firm may ask fewer people to maintain the code. With three weeks saved and few local employers, I could not absorb even a short cut in hours quietly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep an exception list of overnight pay corrections and take it to the agency's scheduled monthly review. If our employer reduces my hours, we'd stop paying for weekend train trips to see friends and put that money toward rent; I'd check for actual paid payroll-clerk vacancies, but apply only where combined wages cover rent, food and my partner's travel to laundry shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing paid hours, and irritated by the idea that a faster answer can settle a wage dispute. I am not going to try an AI tool on real care-worker records without a demonstrated privacy check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is on the care sheet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The overnight sheet has the carer's start time, the client visit and a signature. A dashboard total alone cannot explain whether the last twenty minutes were paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What spending would change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The train trips are pleasant, but our friends can call us. Rent and bus fare to my partner's shifts come first if my hours drop.

say: I'd demand **signed shift evidence** before AI changes a carer's pay.
I'd say **routine payroll code** may reduce paid maintenance hours.
think: I could lose **my hours** despite knowing the care agency's exceptions.
I cannot fund **an income gap** with only three weeks saved.
do: Keep **overnight pay list** for scheduled agency reviews.
Stop **weekend train trips** if developer hours fall and redirect savings to rent.
Apply only to **real paid payroll vacancy** if combined wages cover rent, food and laundry travel.
feel: **Anxious** about hours and the effect of errors on care workers.
S1.quote: A dashboard total alone cannot explain whether the last twenty minutes were paid.
fieldNote: **Timekeeping code and replies** face steady AI change, putting her own paid hours at risk.
She cuts **discretionary travel** only after lost hours and requires an actual payroll vacancy with enough pay.

steps.text: Keep listing overnight pay errors for monthly agency review
Stop weekend train trips after developer-hour cuts and redirect money to rent
Apply to paid payroll vacancy only if combined wages cover rent, food and laundry travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues that thinking AGI by 2028 can write our payroll code before care robots arrive around 2031. I would want every worker to have a way to contest a wrong paid hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my maintenance job could end quickly. My partner's uneven laundry pay will not cover rent and food alone, and three weeks saved would be gone before a slow search found another software post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the care agency and the town hospital about actual paid timekeeping or payroll-office openings and written wages and shifts. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd take a signed job only if the combined pay covers rent, food and transport to both workplaces; if none qualifies, I'd seek any available paid local work and call the landlord before the next rent is due.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I know the midnight rule, but knowing it is not the same as being hired to check it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could you show an employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring an anonymised example of the 12:20 visit and how I corrected the unpaid break. I would leave out the client address and the worker's name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do both rotas matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I need the shift times before accepting an offer. If the new rota makes my partner miss laundry hours, the remaining combined wage must still cover our bills.

say: I'd protect **worker pay appeals** if 2028 thinking AI replaces code.
I'd ask for **written wage terms** and shifts before naming a fallback.
think: I expect **my maintenance post** could end fast.
I cannot cover **rent and food** on uneven laundry pay alone.
do: Ask **care agency and hospital** for actual paid payroll openings, wages and shifts now.
After cut, take only **signed work** whose combined pay covers rent, food and transport after laundry-hour changes.
If none qualifies, seek **available paid local work** and contact landlord before rent is due.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely wage loss and a three-week reserve.
S2.quote: I know the midnight rule, but knowing it is not the same as being hired to check it.
fieldNote: **2028 thinking AGI** reaches payroll code before hands-on care robots around 2031.
Her experience cannot replace **an actual paid vacancy**, signed wage or a workable pair of shifts.

steps.text: Ask care agency and hospital about paid payroll jobs, wages and shifts
Take signed job only if combined wages cover rent, food and transport after laundry-hour changes
If no payroll post qualifies, seek paid work and call landlord before rent is due

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 could let us see whether agencies still pay someone to reconcile care workers' hours. Thinking AI arrives for the code then, and hands-on robots follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not think five years means five guaranteed pay cheques. I am 58 now, retirement is in sight, and I have no verified pension figure that would cover our rent if my job went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the monthly signed-sheet checks and ask the care agency for written requirements and pay for a wage-dispute clerk. If a real vacancy opens and its paid hours with my partner's laundry wages cover rent, food and travel without losing necessary laundry shifts, I'd apply; after 2031 I'd take it only on a signed offer, otherwise keep my developer hours while available and seek other paid local work if they end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though I can learn what the desk job requires while I am still earning. I will not resign for a promise that a clerk's chair may exist someday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What authority would the clerk need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wage-dispute clerk has to call the supervisor when the paper sheet and app disagree, not just press approve. I already know the midnight bug, but I would ask the agency who can authorize a correction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which household numbers matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would want the posted hours and the monthly wage in writing. Laundry work is not a fixed salary, so we would check the actual recent rotas rather than count a perfect week.

I'd say **2031 thinking AI** reaches code before 2034 care robots.
think: I have **no verified pension** and cannot assume five years of wages.
I need **real paid hours** that cover rent with variable laundry income.
do: Keep **signed-sheet reviews** and ask agency for written clerk requirements and pay.

fieldNote: **Five years** permit job research but do not erase her thin cushion or uncertain future wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 might take me to 68, but thinking AI will still reach care-pay code before hands-on robots around 2039. A date does not tell a carer whether the last twenty minutes were paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still have three weeks saved today and my partner's shifts vary. I cannot call retirement affordable until I see actual pension amounts and dates beside our rent and food costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking overnight pay and save the cancelled 22 film fee whenever both wages arrive, then request both retirement statements and compare them with the last six laundry rotas and our rent. In the first year after 2036 I'd stop paid work only if verified income covers rent, food and travel; otherwise I'd keep or seek available paid local work, with no assumption that our children can make up a gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, even with ten years, because the bills are this month's bills. I would like the statement to surprise me, but I will not spend a hopeful number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must the statement show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paperwork has to show a monthly amount and a start date. I would put the figures beside our actual laundry pay slips, not a best-case roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children cover a gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children have their own homes. We would welcome a Sunday visit, but I will not ask them to build our retirement budget.

I'd say **2036 thinking AI** reaches payroll code before 2039 care robots.

I cannot count **unknown pension money** or our children's pay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the payroll maintenance job could end before another local employer pays me to check hours. Written cut notice, real vacancies and shift terms, and an early landlord conversation would help us protect the rent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who loses money when a shift crosses midnight. The carer loses twenty minutes first; I lose the wage later if the firm decides the app no longer needs me.

headlineQuote: The carer loses twenty minutes first; I lose the wage later if the firm decides the app no longer needs me.
portrait: Priya, **58**, is an experienced mid-level care-pay developer with a bachelor's degree who checks overnight wage errors against signed sheets.
Her **lower pay**, variable laundry household income, three-week reserve and few nearby software jobs make ordinary rent pressure serious.
She has **never used AI** and insists a carer's missing minutes need signed evidence and an authorized correction.
Fast 2028 AGI **alarms** her; any payroll move needs an actual vacancy, signed hours and combined pay covering rent and travel.
Even with ten years, she will **verify pension figures** against real laundry rotas and will not use grown children's wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her maintenance wage before another paid local opening appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written cut notice**, real paid vacancies, shift terms and early landlord contact would help protect rent.
